children: Japan's financial leaders pledged to keep a close eye on the yen, saying that currency-market stability is crucial for both the country's inflation and the global economy.

Coordinated foreign-exchange intervention "helps support the stability of global markets and economies," Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said at a news conference held after the Group of 20 financial leaders' summit.

At the meeting, Katayama said she explained the Japanese government's actions in the foreign-exchange market--which it did in coordination with the U.S.--and none of the global financial chiefs expressed disagreement.

Since the U.S. and Japan carried out intervention to prop up the yen, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has talked more publicly about the yen and his confidence in Bank of Japan Gov. Kazuo Ueda's policy-handling--remarks market participants have interpreted as tacit pressure to raise interest rates.

Speaking with Ueda on the sidelines of the G-20 meeting on Sunday, Bessent expressed his support for Japan's decisive steps to address the yen's undervaluation and noted its role in driving domestic inflation, a Treasury statement showed.

Ueda, who was also present at the press briefing with Katayama, said recent economic indicators are in line with the central bank's projections, reiterating his stance to consider further interest-rate hikes based on economic, price and financial conditions.
With Japan's underlying inflation close to the BOJ's target of 2%, the bank should be more careful about the possibility of inflation overshooting, Ueda said.
"Foreign-exchange movements are one upside risk factor that requires close attention," he added.

The yen was last trading at 160.20 against the dollar, remaining close to a 40-year low of nearly 164 after the round of joint intervention failed to reverse the currency's downtrend. The yield on 10-year Japanese government bonds also rose to 3% on Tuesday for the first time since September 1996.

A weak yen threatens to accelerate Japan's inflation, given the country's heavy reliance on imports of energy and food. BOJ policymakers are increasingly worried that underlying inflation could overshoot the target.

title: Japan's Finance Leaders Vow to Keep Eye on Yen as Inflation Fears Rise
